client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just... can't enjoy it the way I used to. It's like there's this hollow feeling in the room where she used to be, and I don't know if talking about it is actually going to make that any better.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds genuinely heavy — that hollow feeling you described is such a real and painful part of grief, and it makes sense that family gatherings bring it rushing forward. I notice there's a part of you that's questioning whether talking will even help, and that doubt is worth sitting with, because sometimes grief can make connection feel pointless when the one person we most want there is missing. What I'd gently offer is that naming that emptiness — just as you did right now — is actually the beginning of honoring both your loss and your love for her.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that, I really do. But it almost feels like... naming it just makes it more real, more present, and I'm not sure I want that right now. Like, what's the point of honoring something when the person you'd want to share that with is just gone?
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly, almost carefully — tells me this is a tender place, like you're holding something fragile and aren't sure you want to press on it too hard. That fear of making the grief *more* real is so understandable, and it's actually a very human form of self-protection. But I want to gently reflect back what you just said — *you* brought her into this room today, which tells me some part of you is already reaching toward her, even while another part is afraid of what that costs.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess you're right that I brought her up... I didn't even really plan to, it just kind of slipped out. But I'm not sure "reaching toward her" is how I'd describe it — it feels more like she's always just there, hovering at the edges of everything, and sometimes the wall I've built gets a little thinner. I don't know if that's the same thing as being ready to actually feel it.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, softly, almost like the words are slipping out before you can catch them — feels very much like what you're describing, that the wall gets thinner sometimes without you choosing it. And I think your distinction matters: there's a difference between *ready* and *happening anyway*, and you don't have to be ready for grief to already be moving through you. Maybe the question isn't whether you're prepared to feel it, but whether you can be a little gentle with yourself when it surfaces on its own.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to accept it, but being gentle with myself feels almost... foreign, like I don't really know what that looks like in practice. When the grief surfaces at the wrong moment, like at work or in the middle of a conversation, my instinct is just to shut it down fast because I can't fall apart there. I guess I'm not sure how to be gentle with something I'm also trying to hold back at the same time.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly but quickly, like you're trying to get the words out before something catches up with you — really mirrors what you're describing, this push-pull between letting something surface and keeping it contained. What you're doing at work isn't weakness or avoidance; it's actually a reasonable adaptation, because *there are* moments when falling apart isn't safe or possible. But I wonder if we could explore what "gentle" might look like in small, manageable ways — not letting it all flood in at once, but maybe just allowing yourself to acknowledge, quietly and privately, *"this is grief, and it makes sense that it's here."*
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible, just quietly naming it without it turning into something I can't control. But honestly, I'm not sure I trust myself to do that, like what if acknowledging it even a little bit is enough to crack something open that I won't be able to close again before my next meeting or before I have to go pick up my kids? It feels less like a gentle door and more like I'm standing in front of something that's been sealed shut for a reason, and I'm scared of what's on the other side.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — your voice quick and pitched high, like something is pressing from the inside — tells me this fear feels very immediate and real, not abstract. And I want to honor that fear, because that sealed door didn't appear for no reason; it was built by *you*, to protect *you*, and that's not something to bulldoze. What I'd offer is this: the goal was never to fling it open, but to trust that you are the one holding the handle — and that you can open it a crack and close it again, on your own terms, in your own time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that — that I'm the one holding the handle. But honestly, it doesn't feel that way most of the time. It feels more like the door has a mind of its own, and if I get too close to it, something on the other side is going to push through before I'm ready.
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, with your voice pitched high — feels like it matches exactly what you're describing, like something is already pressing close just from talking about it. That experience of the door having a mind of its own is actually really common in grief, and it doesn't mean you've lost control; it means the loss was significant enough to live in your body, not just your thoughts. What if we gently explored together what you're actually afraid is on the other side — not to open the door, but just to understand a little more about what you're protecting yourself from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but I'm not sure I want to understand what's behind the door, honestly. Like, what's the point of poking at something that's already managed to stay shut? I guess I'm scared that if I start looking at it too closely, I'll just fall apart and there won't be anyone around to help me put myself back together.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — very quietly, very quickly, like the words are almost escaping before you can stop them — tells me that last part, about there being no one to help put you back together, might be the most important thing you've said today. That fear of falling apart *alone* is so much bigger than the grief itself, and it makes complete sense that the door stays shut when there's no sense of a safe net underneath you. I want you to know that part of what we're building here, slowly, is exactly that — a place where if something does crack open, you won't be facing it by yourself.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that... but I also keep thinking, what happens when the session ends and I'm back in my apartment by myself. Like, this room feels okay right now, but it's such a small island, you know? And I'm not sure one hour a week is enough to make me feel like there's actually a net there when things start to unravel at 2am on a Tuesday.
therapist: The way your voice sounds right now — pitched high but almost eerily calm, like someone standing very still in a big empty space — really captures what you're describing, that quiet, exposed feeling of knowing the session ends and the apartment is waiting. What you're naming is real and important: one hour a week was never meant to be the whole net, and part of our work together is helping you build something that exists *inside* you, not just inside this room. But I also want to gently ask — at 2am on a Tuesday, when things unravel, what does that actually look like for you, and is there anyone at all in your life right now who knows even a little of what you've been carrying?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: At 2am it usually looks like me lying on the floor next to my bed, not even in it, just... on the floor with my phone, scrolling through people's lives on Instagram like that's going to fill something. And no, there's no one who really knows — my sister checks in sometimes but I keep it surface level because I don't want to be the person who's falling apart, you know? I guess I'm afraid if I actually told someone how bad it gets, they'd either panic or pull away, and then I'd have even less than I have now.
therapist: The image of you on the floor at 2am, scrolling through other people's lives to fill something — that's one of the loneliest pictures I've heard in a long time, and the way you're speaking right now, very fast and high, like the words are tumbling out, tells me this is costing you something to say out loud. What strikes me deeply is that you're not actually afraid your sister can't handle your pain — you're afraid that showing her the real weight of it will cost you the little connection you do have, and that fear of losing even that small thread makes complete sense. I want to gently offer that the story you're telling yourself — that honesty will push people away — is worth examining, because you've just shared something really raw with me, and I'm still here.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but you're kind of... required to stay, aren't you? Like, that's your job, so it doesn't quite feel like the same thing as my sister choosing to stay after seeing all of that. And honestly, the fear isn't just about pushing her away — it's that once she really sees how bad it gets, the 2am floor moments, all of it, she'll start looking at me differently, like I'm fragile or broken, and I can't stand the thought of being that person to her.
therapist: You're absolutely right that I'm here professionally, and it matters that you named that — it shows how much the *choice* piece means to you, being seen and still chosen freely. But I want to gently turn something around: the person who lies on the floor at 2am and still gets up, still goes to work, still picks up their kids, still sits here trying to understand herself — that's not a broken person, that's an extraordinarily resilient one. The fear that your sister will see "fragile" is worth questioning, because what if what she actually sees is someone she loves who has been carrying something enormous, completely alone?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
